What did the Micmac story of "bears on floating islands" describe?
column2: It described the Micmacs' first sight of Europeans: a wooden ship with tree trunks planted on it that looked like a floating island, carrying hairy men they took for bears.

column1: How did European metal goods change Indian life in the north?
column2: Iron axes, knives, brass kettles, flint strike-a-lights and metal arrowheads made Indian work easier and their hunters and warriors deadlier, so Indians eagerly allied with European traders.

column1: Why did the Hurons and their allies insist Champlain be a friend and not just a merchant?
column2: For the Montagnais, Algonquins and Hurons, trading goods was bound up in social relations, so a trading partner also had to be an ally, which led Champlain to fight the Mohawks for them.

column1: Who actually trapped and supplied the furs in New France's fur trade?
column2: New France's Indian allies, chiefly the Hurons, Montagnais and Algonquins, supplied tens of thousands of beaver pelts in exchange for European goods, while the few French traded and lived among them.

column1: What did France aim for in North America?
column2: France sought a permanent presence (Port Royal, then Quebec), profits from the fur trade, and the conversion of Indians to Catholicism, while keeping Canada Catholic and closed to French Protestants.

column1: What made the Jesuits successful among New France's Indians?
column2: Champlain insisted from the 1630s that trading partners let the Jesuits live among them, and smallpox deaths then pushed many desperate Hurons to convert and seek baptism.

column1: What did Jesuit conversions do to Huron society?
column2: Jesuit conversions brought visible cultural change and internal divisions that left the Huron confederacy fragmented and vulnerable to its Iroquois enemies.

column1: What caused the Beaver Wars?
column2: The beaver in Iroquois lands collapsed, Mohawk control of the Dutch trade at Fort Orange gave the Iroquois guns, and epidemics drove them to seize Huron furs, hunting grounds and captives to replace their dead.

column1: How did the fur trade change relations among Indian peoples?
column2: Dutch guns let the Iroquois raid Huron convoys and destroy the Hurons, then scatter dozens of other peoples in the Beaver Wars, creating a massive refugee crisis.

column1: How did the Iroquois League gain power in the 1600s?
column2: The five-nation Iroquois confederacy controlled the fur supply to the Dutch at Fort Orange, armed itself with Dutch muskets, destroyed the Hurons and absorbed captives and refugees to replace its dead.

column1: Why did the Dutch want New Netherland?
column2: The Calvinist Dutch, rich and free at home, wanted direct access to North American furs and to compete with Spain, not permanent colonies, so few settlers came.

column1: Why did the Beaver Wars push the French toward the Mississippi?
column2: The wars wrecked Champlain's trading system and scattered refugees westward, so the French sought new Indian partners and took a more expansive view of the continent.

column1: Why did the Indians of the Great Lakes and Mississippi valley welcome French traders?
column2: These peoples wanted French trade goods and help against the Iroquois they feared and hated, and the French also mediated disputes among them.

column1: Along which river did France build the core of New France?
column2: France built its core along the St. Lawrence River, where Cartier first sailed, Champlain founded Quebec, and the towns of Quebec, Montreal and Trois-Rivières stood by 1700.

column1: Why did the French see the Mississippi valley as important?
column2: The French saw the Mississippi valley, draining an area larger than the Indian subcontinent, as the strategic key to North America and hoped its Indian allies would hem in Spain and England.

column1: What contrast does the chapter draw between French and English colonizers?
column2: The French were relatively few and came mainly for trade and converts, while English colonists, spurred in New England by the Protestant Reformation, came in growing numbers and wanted land.

column1: What does the Historian's Toolbox say a colonial map really is?
column2: A map like Franquelin's 1684 Louisiana map is an argument, because what a mapmaker includes, leaves out and labels makes political claims that rival empires and Indians would dispute.

column1: Why did the English come to cold, rocky New England at all?
column2: By 1620 sharper religious quarrels, political tension, unemployment and recession at home produced a mix of desperation and idealism that pushed English people to emigrate.

column1: What did the Puritans object to in the Church of England?
column2: The Puritans objected that the church counted everyone as members, kept Catholic "corruptions" like bishops and ornate vestments, and had too many clergy who could not preach.

column1: How did predestination shape the Puritans' drive to reform society?
column2: Because the Puritans believed an all-powerful God directed history, they strove to play their part in God's plan by reforming church and society along Calvin's lines.

column1: How did the Separatists differ from other Congregationalists?
column2: The Separatists wanted to leave the Church of England because they thought it too corrupt to reform, while most Congregationalists wanted to stay and reform it.

column1: Why did the Separatists leave Holland for America?
column2: Holland gave the Separatists complete religious freedom, but their children were adopting Dutch customs and other religions, so they decided to move again.

column1: Who settled the earliest New England colonies?
column2: Separatist Pilgrims, humble craftworkers and farmers, settled Plymouth, and then larger numbers of Puritan Congregationalists and Presbyterians, including merchants, gentlemen and lawyers, settled Massachusetts Bay.

column1: Why did Plymouth survive its first year?
column2: An epidemic had emptied the coast, so the Wampanoag chief Massasoit, eager for trade and allies, helped the starving Pilgrims through the go-between Squanto.

column1: Why did the Pilgrims write the Mayflower Compact?
column2: The Pilgrims had no royal charter or Crown approval for their land or government, so they wrote their own framework before landing, and distracted English authorities left them alone.

column1: Why did the Massachusetts Bay Puritans move their colony to New England?
column2: Persecuted under Charles I, the Puritans aimed to build an example society for the world and regroup across the Atlantic for another assault on church corruption, not to abandon the English church.

column1: How did John Winthrop envision Massachusetts Bay?
column2: John Winthrop envisioned a godly "city on a hill" that would be an example to the world, whose settlers "must be knit together, in this work, as one man."

column1: How did New England migrants differ from Chesapeake migrants?
column2: New Englanders came in family groups of skilled, literate farmers, artisans and merchants with a balanced sex ratio, while Chesapeake migrants were mostly young single indentured servants.

column1: How did religion shape New England's government and community life?
column2: Tax-supported churches were the center of community life and policed morality, church membership at first decided who could vote, and settlers sought an ordered society modeled on Scripture, though ministers held no civil office.

column1: What were the sources of stability in early New England?
column2: Family migration, long lives, rough equality of land, strong fathers, shared Puritan churches and broad self-government in town meetings and elected assemblies kept early New England stable.

column1: What were the sources of conflict in early New England?
column2: Fervent disagreement over how to apply the Bible bred dissenters and breakaway colonies, fear of independent women fed witchcraft accusations, and hunger for land led to wars with the Indians.

column1: Why were Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson threats to the Puritan leaders?
column2: Williams attacked ties to the Church of England, church-state union and the king's land charter, while Hutchinson, a woman teaching her own doctrine, challenged the ministers' authority and was branded a heretic.

column1: Who was most likely to be accused of witchcraft in New England?
column2: Most accused witches were women, usually middle-aged or older and seen as too independent, often previously suspected of heresy or sexual impropriety, or heirs to property.

column1: What happened in the Salem witch hysteria?
column2: In 1692 a group of Salem Village girls' fortune-telling went sour, their fits were blamed on witchcraft, hundreds were accused and twenty innocent people executed until ministers protested.

column1: How did historians explain the Salem witch trials?
column2: Historians point to Puritan mistrust of independent women, rivalries among Salem Village families, links between the accused and Quakers, and trauma from wars with Indians and the French.

column1: What place did women have in New England churches?
column2: Women could not be ministers but became the majority of church members after the 1660s and sometimes voted on ministers and members, though the ideal woman was a submissive helpmeet.

column1: How did New England colonists get Indian land?
column2: Colonists bought land (sometimes fairly, sometimes by fraud or force), moved onto lands emptied by epidemics, and joined Indian wars to seize territory.

column1: What weaknesses did New England's Indians face against the colonists?
column2: Epidemics had killed up to 90 percent of coastal peoples, power was local to each village sachem, and rival nations' feuds let the English play them against one another.

column1: What brought about the Pequot War, and how did it end?
column2: Seeking land by joining Indian rivalries, colonists allied with the Narragansetts against the Pequots, who controlled Connecticut territory, and ended the war by burning the main Pequot village, killing hundreds.

column1: What did Roger Williams warn about English land hunger?
column2: Roger Williams warned that "God Land" would be as great a god to the English as "God Gold" was to the Spaniards.

column1: Why did Metacom go to war in 1675?
column2: Metacom believed his nation could survive only by war, because colonists humiliated the Wampanoags, their livestock ruined Indian fields, praying towns split the tribe, and the English plotted to replace sachems.

column1: Why did Metacom lose his war?
column2: Metacom ran short of food and ammunition and failed to win over the Mohegans and Mohawks, who sided with the English, so the tide turned in 1676.

column1: How did the English take New Netherland?
column2: The Dutch West India Company had gone bankrupt and virtually abandoned the colony, so the Dutch surrendered on the mere arrival of the Duke of York's invading fleet in 1664.

column1: In what ways were the mid-Atlantic colonies more diverse than other colonies?
column2: The mid-Atlantic mixed Dutch, English, French, Swedes, Finns, Germans, Africans and Jews with Dutch Reformed, Quaker, Lutheran, Catholic and other faiths, lacking New England's common bonds.

column1: What happened to New Jersey after it was founded?
column2: Berkeley and Carteret split it into East and West Jersey and sold both to Quakers, who resold them, leaving a patchwork of small farms that the Crown reunited as a royal colony.

column1: What practices set the Quakers apart?
column2: Quakers dressed plainly, refused to bow, kneel or remove hats for superiors, refused oaths and war, and let women preach, because all share equally in the Light Within.

column1: Why did Charles II give William Penn Pennsylvania?
column2: Charles II may have been repaying a large loan from Penn's father to the Stuarts or hoping to send England's Quakers to a colony run by a trusted friend.

column1: How did Penn's Pennsylvania differ from Puritan Massachusetts on religion?
column2: Penn's Frame of Government guaranteed complete freedom of worship, while Puritan Massachusetts taxed everyone for its churches, tied voting to church membership and expelled dissenters.

column1: How did William Penn treat the Lenni Lenapes?
column2: Penn bought land from the Lenapes before selling it to settlers, banned alcohol sales to them, regulated the fur trade and learned their language, believing they rightfully owned the land.

column1: Why did Pennsylvania have scattered farms and county government?
column2: Commercial wheat farming needed larger farms, and peace with the Lenapes meant farmers did not need to cluster, so the county, not the town, became the unit of local government.

column1: Why was Pennsylvania politics full of strife?
column2: Rich investors controlled the council that alone proposed laws, the assembly fought for that power, farmers resented Penn's quitrents, and the Lower Counties wanted to separate.

column1: Why did the king want more control over the colonies by the 1680s?
column2: The colonies had few ties to the English state: Chesapeake planters grumbled at tobacco duties, New Englanders ignored the Navigation Acts and traded with the Dutch, and proprietors faced defiance.

column1: Why did the Dominion of New England collapse?
column2: James II's Catholicism and attempt to rule without Parliament led Parliament to overthrow him in the Glorious Revolution, and William and Mary dismantled the Dominion.

column1: What did the Glorious Revolution change in the colonies?
column2: William and Mary restored the northern colonies' elected assemblies and gave Connecticut and Rhode Island back their charters, and Massachusetts received a new royal charter.

column1: What did Massachusetts' 1691 charter change?
column2: The charter joined Massachusetts, Plymouth and Maine as a royal colony with a Crown-appointed governor, imposed religious toleration, and based voting on property instead of church membership.

column1: How did William and Mary try to increase colonial revenues?
column2: In 1696 they added customs officials in every colony, set up jury-less vice-admiralty courts to try smugglers, and created the Board of Trade, channeling colonial trade through England.

column1: How could laws be vetoed in a royal colony?
column2: The royal council could veto any assembly law, the governor could veto laws passed by both houses, and the Crown could veto laws the governor had approved.

column1: What had the colonies become by 1700, according to the text?
column2: By 1700 the colonies were becoming firmly rooted societies whose laws and traditions rested on both English inheritance and American conditions, which blocked Stuart, proprietor and reformer designs.

column1: Why was royal power in the colonies "more apparent than real" after 1700?
column2: The Glorious Revolution made Parliament supreme in England, and colonial assemblies grew skilled at handling governors and fiercely guarded the lower houses' power to levy taxes.

column1: Why did the dream of empire revive among English rulers?
column2: France never gave up its imperial vision, so England, France and Spain waged a quarter-century "cold war" in North America, knowing distant clashes could affect feuds in Europe.

column1: Why could France and Spain hope to compete with Britain's far larger colonies?
column2: Indians were still the majority population and controlled over 90 percent of North America, so French and Spanish officials hoped Indian alliances would help them prevail.
